content.text: {"predictors": [{"name": "Inventory-to-Sales Acceleration", "construction": "For each firm, compute the ratio of inventories (Compustat item INVT) to sales (SALE) at fiscal year-end. Measure the change in this ratio from year t-1 to t minus the change from year t-2 to t-1 (second difference, i.e., acceleration). Rank cross-sectionally each June using the most recent fiscal year data.", "rationale": "Accelerating inventory buildup relative to sales signals demand overestimation and future markdowns, so managers who let inventory accelerate destroy value that the market underappreciates.", "higher_returns_for": "low values of the measure (decelerating/shrinking inventory-to-sales)"}, {"name": "Depreciation Rate Change", "construction": "Compute depreciation expense (DP) divided by gross PP&E (PPEGT) for each fiscal year. Take the year-over-year change in this depreciation rate. Rank stocks cross-sectionally each June.", "rationale": "A declining depreciation rate can signal earnings management that inflates current profits by stretching asset lives, so firms lowering their depreciation rate should subsequently underperform.", "higher_returns_for": "high values of the measure (rising depreciation rate)"}, {"name": "Dispersion of Segment Profitability", "construction": "Using Compustat business segment data, compute for each firm the sales-weighted standard deviation of operating margin (segment operating profit / segment sales) across reported segments. Standardize by number of segments. Rank annually.", "rationale": "Firms with widely dispersed segment margins likely cross-subsidize weak divisions, indicating agency-driven capital misallocation that depresses future returns.", "higher_returns_for": "low values of the measure (uniform segment profitability)"}, {"name": "Order Backlog to Market Cap", "construction": "Take reported order backlog (Compustat item OB when available) divided by market capitalization at fiscal year-end. Rank cross-sectionally each June among firms reporting backlog.", "rationale": "A large backlog relative to price represents contracted future revenue the market fails to fully capitalize, generating positive drift as backlog converts to sales.", "higher_returns_for": "high values of the measure"}, {"name": "Trading Volume Concentration", "construction": "Using daily CRSP volume over the prior 12 months, compute the Herfindahl index of monthly volume shares (sum of squared monthly volume fractions). Higher values mean volume is concentrated in few months. Rank cross-sectionally monthly.", "rationale": "Concentrated trading indicates episodic informed-trading events and lower steady-state liquidity, so investors demand a premium for holding such stocks.", "higher_returns_for": "high values of the measure"}, {"name": "Accrual-Cashflow Divergence Persistence", "construction": "For each firm compute earnings minus operating cash flow (total accruals, scaled by total assets) for each of the last three fiscal years. Count the number of consecutive years accruals exceeded the firm's own trailing median. Rank annually.", "rationale": "Persistently high accruals relative to cash generation reflect entrenched aggressive accounting or deteriorating quality, predicting mean-reversion in earnings and lower returns.", "higher_returns_for": "low values of the measure (few consecutive high-accrual years)"}, {"name": "Relative R&D Momentum", "construction": "Compute R&D expense (XRD) scaled by sales for each firm, then take the two-year growth rate in this ratio. Within each industry (SIC 3-digit), demean the growth rate. Rank cross-sectionally each June.", "rationale": "Firms increasing R&D intensity faster than industry peers are building intangible capital that is expensed immediately and undervalued, yielding delayed positive returns.", "higher_returns_for": "high values of the measure"}, {"name": "Dividend Smoothing Deviation", "construction": "Estimate each firm's dividend payout as dividends (DVC) over earnings (IB). Compute the absolute deviation of the current-year payout ratio from the firm's trailing five-year average payout ratio. Rank annually among dividend payers.", "rationale": "Large deviations from a firm's established payout policy signal financial stress or unstable cash flows that the market underprices, so stable payers outperform.", "higher_returns_for": "low values of the measure (stable payout)"}, {"name": "Return Skewness Asymmetry", "construction": "Using daily CRSP returns over the past 12 months, compute the ratio of the average of positive daily returns to the absolute average of negative daily returns (gain/loss asymmetry). Rank cross-sectionally monthly.", "rationale": "Investors overpay for lottery-like stocks with large positive skewness in daily returns, so high positive-asymmetry stocks subsequently earn lower returns.", "higher_returns_for": "low values of the measure (negative/less positive skew)"}, {"name": "Working Capital Efficiency Trend", "construction": "Compute the cash conversion cycle = days inventory (INVT/COGS*365) + days receivable (RECT/SALE*365) - days payable (AP/COGS*365) for each fiscal year. Take the three-year change (improvement is negative change). Rank cross-sectionally each June.", "rationale": "Firms improving operational efficiency by shortening their cash conversion cycle free up capital and signal better management, predicting higher future returns.", "higher_returns_for": "low values of the measure (shrinking cash conversion cycle)"}]}
